Build the composite "Albers USA" projection: the continental US via
albers, with Alaska and Hawaii drawn as scaled insets in the
lower-left, the standard US thematic-map layout. Each region uses its own

the composite frame, so the three regions never overlap.

box, else the continental projection. The continental US is centered on the
origin.

symbols.name: AnimateChoropleth
symbols.summary:
AnimateChoropleth: tween a ChoroplethMap's region fills from their
current colors to the colors for a new set of values.

This is the "choropleth over time" animation: give it the map and a new value
accessor, and every region's fill crossfades from its present color to the
color the new value maps to. Colors are blended with interpolateColor
(the same RGB blend the rest of the library uses). It mirrors
FadeToColor, but drives each region's fill (not a single stroke color)
and reads its targets from the map's own value/color/domain logic.

The GIF is decoded to RGBA frames (see gifDecoder) and each frame is

signatures.summary:
Bind a mobject to a live 2x2 matrix so it morphs continuously.

Every VMobject leaf in `target`'s family is snapshotted at bind time. An
updater is added to `target`; each frame it re-maps every snapshotted point
by the current matrix (about `aboutPoint`) and moves any dependent points.
Because the re-map always starts from the snapshot, the transform is absolute
and free of per-frame drift — a collapsed (singular) matrix is just a flat
grid, with full recovery on the next frame.

The one-shot `applyMatrix` is untouched; this is the additive live mode.

symbols.summary:
ApplyPointwiseFunctionToCenter animation -- applies a pointwise function
relative to each mobject's center rather than absolute coordinates.

For each VMobject in the family tree it:
1. Shifts all points so the mobject's center is at the origin
2. Applies the user-supplied pointwise function
3. Shifts back to the original center

This is useful for applying the same transformation (e.g. scaling, rotation)
to multiple mobjects, each relative to its own center.

symbols.name: ArcPolygonFromArcs
symbols.summary:
ArcPolygonFromArcs - a closed path stitched from pre-made Arc pieces.

Port of Manim CE's `ArcPolygonFromArcs`. Each arc's points are appended in
order; between one arc's last point and the next arc's first point a
connecting straight segment is inserted, subdivided to roughly match the arc
resolution. The arcs are taken in cyclic order, so the final segment closes
the path back to the first arc's first point. Endpoints are read from the
arcs' actual geometry (first and last points), matching CE's `get_start`
and `get_end`. The arcs' endpoints are assumed to connect; when they do, the
connecting segments are degenerate and the result is one continuous path.

Unlike CE this does not also add the arcs as child submobjects: the result is
only the stitched path, so the arcs are not drawn a second time.

symbols.name: BohrDiagram
symbols.summary:
BohrDiagram - a 2D Bohr-model (electron-shell) diagram of an atom.

A Bohr diagram shows a central nucleus and a set of concentric electron
shells. Each shell carries the number of electrons that textbook Bohr
diagrams place in it. The nucleus shows the element symbol and the proton
count.

Shell filling uses the simple 2n^2 shell-capacity rule: shell 1 holds up to
2, shell 2 up to 8, shell 3 up to 18, shell 4 up to 32, and each shell is
filled before the next begins. This is a deliberate simplification. Real
Bohr diagrams follow the "2, 8, 8, 18" convention, so from potassium
(Z = 19) onward the two rules differ (for example this rule gives potassium
[2, 8, 9], while the textbook 2-8-8 rule gives [2, 8, 8, 1]). Pass the
`shells` option to set the per-shell counts directly when the exact textbook
filling is needed.

The diagram is a VGroup, so Create and FadeIn animate it directly.
examples:
```typescript
const carbon = new BohrDiagram({ element: 'C' });   // shells [2, 4]
const sodium = new BohrDiagram({ element: 'Na' });  // shells [2, 8, 1]
scene.play(new Create(carbon));
```

symbols.summary:
How `Camera2D.setAspectRatio` reconciles the user-set frame with the
viewport's pixel aspect.

- `'fill'` (default): keep `frameHeight`, recompute `frameWidth` from
  the viewport aspect. Frame is cropped horizontally on wider viewports
  and over-shows on narrower ones. Back-compatible.
- `'contain'`: keep both base `frameWidth` and `frameHeight`. Grow
  whichever dimension is needed to letterbox so the user's full
  frame is always visible (no cropping of the intended view).

symbols.name: CameraFrame
symbols.summary:
CameraFrame - ManimGL-style camera frame with Euler angle control and animation support.

Provides programmatic camera animation via:
  frame.incrementPhi(PI/4)         // tilt up (immediate)
  frame.incrementTheta(PI/4)       // orbit right (immediate)
  scene.play(frame.animate.incrementPhi(PI/4))  // smooth tilt
  scene.play(frame.animate.setEulerAngles({ theta: PI/4, phi: PI/3 }))

Euler angle convention (matching ManimGL):
  theta = azimuthal angle (horizontal orbit in XZ plane)
  phi   = polar angle (vertical tilt from Y axis, 0 = top, PI = bottom)
  gamma = roll angle (rotation around the viewing axis)

signatures.summary:
Compute the arcs and ribbons of a chord diagram.

Group `i`'s arc angle is proportional to the sum of row `i`. The cell
`matrix[i][j]` is a sub-span on arc `i`; a ribbon joins the span `(i, j)` on
arc `i` to the span `(j, i)` on arc `j`. One ribbon is produced per unordered
pair whose combined flow is positive, including a self-ribbon when the
diagonal is positive.

The function never throws. An empty matrix returns empty arrays, and an
all-zero matrix returns zero-angle arcs and no ribbons.

In ManimCE (`manim/mobject/graphing/coordinate_systems.py`) `CoordinateSystem`
is the abstract base of `Axes` and `NumberPlane`. manim-web does not need that
class hierarchy, because `Axes` is concrete and `NumberPlane extends Axes`.

share, so callers can program against the abstraction. `Axes` declares
`implements CoordinateSystem`, so the compiler checks the surface stays in
sync, and `NumberPlane` inherits it.

symbols.name: DensitySurface
symbols.summary:
DensitySurface - a 3D isosurface extracted from a scalar density grid.

A density grid is a flat array of scalar samples on a regular 3D lattice: a
cryo-EM map, an electron-density map, or any volumetric field. DensitySurface
is a Group that holds one ImplicitSurface: it wraps the grid in
a trilinear-interpolating sampler `f(x, y, z)` and lets marching cubes extract
the level set `f = isoValue` over the grid's world bounding box.

## The grid

The grid is cell-centered. Voxel `(i, j, k)` has its center at world position

```
origin + (i + 0.5, j + 0.5, k + 0.5) * spacing
```

so each voxel occupies a cell of size `spacing`, and the whole grid spans the
world box `[origin, origin + dims * spacing]`. Values are stored flat with
index `x + nx * (y + ny * z)` (x fastest), matching the common C-order of map
files.

## The sampler (trilinear, bounded)

The sampler maps a world point to continuous voxel-center coordinates
`v = (p - origin) / spacing - 0.5`, then trilinearly interpolates the eight
surrounding grid values. At a voxel center `v` is an integer, so the sampler
returns that voxel's value exactly; between centers it interpolates.

Outside the voxel-center lattice (any axis `v < 0` or `v > dim - 1`) the
sampler returns the grid's minimum value. For a density map the minimum is the
background (near 0), which is below a positive iso value. This keeps the field
low at the box faces, so the isosurface closes inside the box and never shuts
against a box face. MolecularSurface documents the same box-blob
failure for a field that stays above its threshold across the whole box; a
field that drops to the background at the lattice edge avoids it.

## The iso value

The default iso value is `0.5 * max(values)`, half the peak density. This is a
common first choice for an electron-density or cryo-EM isosurface: it sits
between the background (low) and the peak, so the surface wraps the dense core.
Pass an explicit `isoValue` to carve the map tighter (higher) or looser
(lower).

symbols.name: DNAHelix
symbols.summary:
DNAHelix - a double helix of DNA.

The helix is two phosphate backbone strands (parametric helices, half a turn
out of phase) plus base-pair "rungs" that connect them at even intervals.
The rungs can be colored by base with the A/T/G/C palette, and a nucleotide
bead sits where each rung meets a backbone.

The helix axis is vertical. A full turn rises by `pitch`, so a helix of
`turns` turns has height `turns * pitch`. In 2D schematic mode the axis is Y
and the strands are two sine waves in the XY plane. In 3D mode the axis is Z
(a ThreeDScene is Z-up), the strands wind around it in the XY plane, and the
nucleotide beads are real spheres.

Depth cue: even in 2D the helix fakes depth. Each rung and bead gets a
"frontness" from the helix angle, so the ones at the back of a turn are
thinner and dimmer than the ones at the front. The eye reads the twist as 3D.

The helix is a VGroup, so Create and FadeIn animate it directly.

symbols.name: DomainColoring
symbols.summary:
DomainColoring - a phase portrait of a complex function f: C -> C.

The region of the complex plane is sampled on a regular pixel grid. Each
pixel's complex value w = f(z) is turned into a color by phasePortraitColor: the hue encodes arg(w) and the brightness encodes |w|.
The pixels are written to an RGBA buffer that is uploaded as a texture on a
flat quad spanning `reRange` x `imRange`, mirroring the way HeatMap
renders a sampled scalar field.

The pixel buffer is computed in plain TypeScript, so it is deterministic and
readable without a browser. In a browser the buffer becomes a
`THREE.CanvasTexture`; without a DOM it becomes an equivalent
`THREE.DataTexture`.

Pixel layout: row 0 is the top (im = imMax), the last row is the bottom
(im = imMin); column 0 is the left (re = reMin), the last column is the
right (re = reMax).

symbols.name: ElectronPushingArrow
symbols.summary:
ElectronPushingArrow - a curved electron-pushing (arrow-pushing) arrow for
2D reaction mechanisms.

Organic chemists draw reaction mechanisms with curved arrows that show where
electrons move: a double-barbed arrow for an electron pair (2 electrons) and
a single-barbed "fishhook" for a single electron (1 electron, radical steps).
The tail sits on the electron source (a lone pair, a bond midpoint or an
atom); the head points at the destination (an atom, a bond or a point).

The arrow is a smooth curved arc from `from` to `to`. The arc bows away from
the straight chord by `bulge` (a fraction of the chord length) to the chosen
`direction` side. The shaft is a single quadratic Bezier, converted to one
cubic segment, so the arc apex lands exactly `bulge * chordLength` off the
chord midpoint. The head is a reused geometry tip primitive.

The arrow is a VMobject whose own points are the shaft and whose single child
is the head, so `Create` draws it progressively (shaft then head) and the
usual Mobject transforms position it.

Shaft reuse note: the repository's `ArcBetweenPoints` / `CurvedArrow` arc math
does not return a path whose end anchor equals the requested end point, so it
cannot drive a from->to shaft. A quadratic Bezier is used instead; it gives an
exact, testable apex offset. The head reuses ArrowTriangleFilledTip.

fields.name: color

fields.name: direction
fields.doc: Which side the arc bows to. Default: 'ccw'.

fields.name: from

fields.name: strokeWidth

and drawn with the same primitive the rest of the 2D geo module uses (an open
Polygon stroke), so Create reveals it progressively like every
other geo line.

Use it for migration, trade or route flows laid over a ChoroplethMap.

Coordinate convention: endpoints are `[latitude, longitude]` in degrees, the
same LatLon order Globe uses. The projection takes
`[longitude, latitude]`, so FlowArc swaps the pair before projecting.

symbols.name: FourierCoefficient
symbols.summary:
A single Fourier coefficient expressed in polar form.

The complex coefficient is `amplitude * e^(i * phase)`. In an epicycle
drawing each coefficient is one rotating vector: `amplitude` is the circle
radius, `phase` is the starting angle, and `freq` is the signed number of
turns the vector makes per unit of normalized time `t`.

fields.name: amplitude
fields.doc: Non-negative magnitude |c_k| (the rotating-vector length / circle radius).

fields.name: freq
fields.doc: Signed integer frequency (…, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, …), centered around 0.

fields.name: phase
fields.doc: Phase arg(c_k) in radians, in (-π, π].

params.name: samples
params.doc: Complex path samples, equally spaced over one period.

signatures.summary:
Compute the discrete Fourier coefficients of a list of complex samples.

Given `N` samples `f[0..N-1]` taken at equal spacing over one period, the
coefficient for index `k` is:

  c_k = (1 / N) * Σ_n f[n] * e^(-2πi · k · n / N)

The returned array has one entry per `k` (DC term first, index `k = 0`).
Each entry carries a *centered* signed frequency: indices in the upper half
(`k > N/2`) map to the negative frequency `k - N`. Centered frequencies make
the vectors rotate in their natural slow-to-fast, alternating-direction
order while still reconstructing every sample exactly (see
reconstructSample).

FourierEpicycles - the rotating-vector ("epicycle") approximation of a path.

Given a path and a number of terms `N`, this builds the chain of `N` rotating
vectors (and their circles) whose tip-to-tail sum tracks the path, plus the
curve traced by the final tip. An updater rotates each vector at its own
frequency and extends the traced curve over time, reproducing the iconic
3Blue1Brown Fourier-series animation.

The geometry is deterministic: setTime fully determines every vector,
circle, and the tip for a given normalized time `t`.

symbols.name: GamepadInput
symbols.summary:
GamepadInput — a general-purpose gamepad controller for interactive apps and
games, built on the Web Gamepad API.

manim-web already has a KeyboardInput for keyboard-driven games. A
gamepad is the other half of game input, and the Web Gamepad API is a
browser-unique capability that file-based ManimCE cannot offer. This
controller is the sibling of KeyboardInput: the same lifecycle
(`enable` / `disable` / `dispose`), the same per-frame edge queries
(`wasButtonPressed` / `wasButtonReleased`), a movement vector from the d-pad
or left stick, and the same `StateMachine` / `ValueTracker` bindings.

The Gamepad API is poll-based: button state arrives in a snapshot, not as
events. So GamepadInput.poll (aliased by GamepadInput.update)
reads the live snapshot each frame and computes the press / release edges.
Call it once per frame before reading state.

All navigator and DOM access is feature-detected, so the controller is safe
to construct in Node, jsdom, or a headless render. Without `getGamepads` the
reads return `false` or zero and nothing throws. Tests inject a fake snapshot
through the `getGamepads` seam, so no real hardware is required.

signatures.summary:
Smooth cubic-Bezier handles for a sequence of anchors (open spline).

Solves the tridiagonal system for a C1-continuous spline through the anchors
(the classic "smooth bezier spline" formulation that Manim CE's
`get_smooth_handle_points` computes). For each internal anchor the incoming
second handle and outgoing first handle are reflections through the anchor,
giving tangent continuity.

Closed paths are smoothed as an open spline over the repeated-endpoint
anchor list, so the seam is not periodic-smooth.

symbols.name: Globe
symbols.summary:
Globe: a 3D sphere for geographic data, with helpers to place lat/long
points, draw great-circle arcs, and build a lat/long graticule.

The globe is a Group holding a sphere plus whatever markers, arcs and
grid the caller adds. The sphere is a plain Sphere by default, or a
texturedSphere when a `textureUrl` is given (the existing texture
path, so an Earth image maps straight on).

Coordinate convention (Z up, matching the rest of the 3D module and the
textured-sphere UV mapping): latitude drives Z (north pole at +Z), longitude
sweeps the X/Y plane from +X (lon 0) toward +Y (lon 90E):
  `x = r cos(lat) cos(lon)`, `y = r cos(lat) sin(lon)`, `z = r sin(lat)`.

signatures.signature: interpolateColorOklab(color1: string, color2: string, alpha: number): string
signatures.summary:
Interpolate two colors in Oklab space and return the result as a hex string.

This is the perceptual counterpart of interpolateColor. `alpha` of
0.0 yields `color1`, 1.0 yields `color2`. The midpoint stays bright and
vivid instead of passing through a muddy linear-RGB blend.

signatures.signature: interpolateColorOklch(color1: string, color2: string, alpha: number): string
signatures.summary:
Interpolate two colors in Oklch space and return the result as a hex string.

This blends lightness and chroma linearly, and hue along the shortest arc of
the color circle. `alpha` of 0.0 yields `color1`, 1.0 yields `color2`. The
result tracks a natural hue sweep, so a red-to-green blend stays saturated
through orange instead of graying out.

When one endpoint is achromatic (chroma near 0), its hue is undefined, so the
hue of the other endpoint is used to avoid an arbitrary sweep.

symbols.name: KeyboardInput
symbols.summary:
KeyboardInput — a general-purpose keyboard controller for interactive apps
and games.

manim-web already has pointer interaction (`Clickable` / `Draggable` /
`Hoverable`) and a `StateMachine`, but no general keyboard primitive. This
controller tracks held keys, exposes per-frame edge queries (`wasPressed` /
`wasReleased`), derives a movement vector from arrow keys and WASD, and binds
a key to a `StateMachine` input or a `ValueTracker`. It makes the kind of
interactive software and games that plain Manim cannot do first-class in the
browser.

in Node, jsdom, or a headless render. Without a window the reads return

symbols.name: ManimColor
symbols.summary:
Class layer ported from ManimCE's `manim/utils/color/core.py` (ManimCE 0.22.0).

The free color functions (hex/rgb/hsv conversion, interpolation, gradients)
live in `./color` and use the 0.0..1.0 float convention. This module adds the
`ManimColor` object on top of them.

manim-web otherwise stores a color as a `#rrggbb` hex string end to end, so a
`ManimColor` stays interoperable by exposing ManimColor.toHex: the
returned string works everywhere the repo expects a color.

Deliberate divergences from ManimCE (documented for parity readers):
- TypeScript cannot tell an integer tuple from a float tuple at run time, so a
  numeric array is always read as a float RGB(A) array in 0.0..1.0. ManimCE's
  int-vs-float auto-detection is not reproduced.
- RandomColorGenerator is deterministic for a given seed, but it does
  not reproduce CPython's Mersenne Twister sequence; it uses a `mulberry32`
  PRNG instead.

symbols.name: MasterTimeline
symbols.summary:
MasterTimeline - Extended Timeline with segment + slide tracking for Player.

Two granularities:
- **Segment**: one play() or wait() call. Pure timing unit.
- **Slide**: one or more contiguous segments that the user navigates as a
  single unit in slidesMode. Mirrors manim-slides' next_slide() concept.

Slides are built by the recorder calling beginSlide(opts) as a boundary
marker; finalizeSlides() at end of recording builds the _slides array.
If no boundary is ever recorded each segment becomes its own slide, which
preserves the original per-play slidesMode behavior.

symbols.name: MathTex
symbols.summary:
MathTex - Vector-based LaTeX rendering using SVG paths (default).

Unlike MathTexImage (which rasterizes LaTeX to a canvas texture), MathTex
produces real VMobject paths from MathJax SVG output. This enables
path-based animations like Create (stroke-draw reveal), DrawBorderThenFill,
and point-morphing Transform.

This is the default LaTeX renderer, matching Python Manim's behavior.

Uses renderLatexToSVG() -> svgToVMobjects() pipeline.

symbols.name: MathTexImage
symbols.summary:
MathTexImage - Rasterized LaTeX rendering for manimweb using KaTeX (default) or MathJax (fallback)

This module provides LaTeX math rendering capabilities by:
1. Using KaTeX to render LaTeX to HTML (fast, limited subset)
2. Falling back to MathJax SVG output for unsupported LaTeX (full LaTeX support)
3. Converting output to canvas via DOM walking / SVG foreignObject
4. Creating a THREE.js textured plane mesh

Renderer selection:
- 'katex'  : KaTeX only (fast, limited subset)
- 'mathjax': MathJax only (slower, full LaTeX including \usepackage, align, etc.)
- 'auto'   : Try KaTeX first; fall back to MathJax if KaTeX throws (default)

NOTE: This is the rasterized (texture-based) renderer. For SVG path-based
rendering (recommended), use MathTex from './MathTex' instead.

Base class for 3D mesh mobjects (Cube, Sphere, Cylinder, Arrow3D, Polyhedron, …).

Unlike VMobjects, a 3D mesh stores its geometry in a Three.js buffer rather
than in bakeable points, so it cannot fold a transform into geometry. Instead
of resetting its local transform to identity (which would silently discard
rotation/scale), `normalizeTransform()` *absolutizes*: it sets the local
transform equal to the incoming world matrix, so the mesh renders in the right
place once its ancestors collapse to identity. It is a flattening barrier — its
descendants stay relative to it. See Mobject._flattenAsMesh.

symbols.name: ModelMobject
symbols.summary:
ModelMobject - import an external 3D model (glTF / .glb / .obj) as a mobject.

ManimCE has no way to import an external 3D model (see the long-standing
"OBJ Support" request). Three.js ships loaders for the common formats, so
manim-web exposes them through a mobject that drops the loaded
`THREE.Object3D` into the normal Group/Mobject hierarchy. The model then
participates in shift / scale / rotate, z-depth and the 3D camera exactly
like a built-in primitive (Cube, Surface3D, ...).

Scene-graph wiring (why there are nested groups):
  wrapper      - returned as `_threeObject`; its local transform is written
                 by `Mobject._syncToThree` from the mobject transform, so it
                 must stay under manim's control alone.
    content    - carries the `scale` and `upAxis` options.
      center   - carries the `center` recenter offset.
        model  - the pristine loaded Object3D (never mutated by options, so
                 `copy()` can clone it and re-apply the options cleanly).

The real Three.js example loaders are pulled in through a lazy dynamic
`import()` on first use, so the base bundle and SSR never load them. Tests
inject a loader (via the `loader` option or `setModelLoaderFactory`), which
bypasses the import and the network entirely - mirroring the
`setTypstCompiler` dependency-injection seam in TypstRenderer.

symbols.name: MolecularSurface
symbols.summary:
MolecularSurface - a smooth 3D molecular surface (the "blobby" surface).

A molecular surface is the shape of a molecule as a single translucent skin,
the kind that shows a drug-binding pocket's cavity. MolecularSurface is a
Group that holds one ImplicitSurface: it samples a metaball
scalar field over the atom bounding box and extracts the isosurface with
marching cubes.

Two kinds of surface are supported:
 - `'vdw'`: the union of van der Waals spheres (the space-filling surface).
 - `'sas'`: the solvent-accessible surface, the van der Waals radius plus a
   probe radius (water, 1.4 angstrom), so the skin sits one water molecule out.

## The scalar field

The field is a signed union-of-spheres distance:

```
f(p) = min_i ( |p - p_i| - r_i )
```

where `p_i` is atom `i`'s world position and `r_i` is its world radius. The
surface is the level set `f = isoValue`, with `isoValue = 0` by default, so
the surface is exactly the union of the atoms' van der Waals spheres. A
positive `isoValue` dilates the surface outward (like a probe); a negative one
shrinks it toward the atom centers.

A summed metaball field (`Σ r_i² / |p - p_i|²`) was tried first but is wrong
for a molecule: the contributions accumulate over many atoms, so the field can
stay above its threshold across the whole sampling box and marching cubes then
closes the surface off at the box faces, producing a box-shaped blob instead of
a molecular skin. The signed distance is local to the nearest atom and has no
such accumulation.

The marching cubes mesher labels a grid corner "inside" when its value is below
the iso level (see marchingCubes); here that is the sphere interior
(`f < 0`), so the surface normals point outward and the shaded skin is correct.

## Performance

Resolution 48 over a small bounding box (a ligand or one pocket) samples
`49³ ≈ 118k` grid points and is fine. A whole protein spans a much larger box,
so the same resolution would undersample it or, if raised, cost `O(n³)` field
evaluations. For a large structure lower the resolution, or split the atoms
into chunks and build one surface per chunk (not implemented here).

symbols.name: OrbitalSurface
symbols.summary:
OrbitalSurface - 3D atomic-orbital lobes drawn as isosurfaces.

An OrbitalSurface shows the recognizable shape of an atomic orbital (an s
blob, a p dumbbell, a d four-lobe or ring-and-lobe) so a reaction can be seen
"at the orbital level". It is a Group that holds one
ImplicitSurface per colored lobe set: marching cubes extracts each
lobe from a scalar field and the lobe is colored by its phase (sign of the
wavefunction).

## The scalar field

Each orbital uses an analytic hydrogen-like shape, a radial gaussian envelope
times the angular part. The full radial wavefunction is not needed; only the
lobe shape must read. The signed shape is:

```
S(p) = angular(p) * exp(-|p - center|^2 / scale^2)
```

where `angular` is `1` for s, a coordinate for p (for example `z/scale` for
pz), and a quadratic form for d (for example `(2z^2 - x^2 - y^2)/scale^2` for
dz2). `S` is positive in one phase and negative in the opposite phase.

One colored lobe set is the region where `sign * S > isoValue`, with
`sign = +1` for the positive phase and `sign = -1` for the negative phase.
The field passed to ImplicitSurface is therefore:

```
f(p) = isoValue - sign * S(p)
```

and the surface is the zero level set `f = 0`. Inside the lobe `f < 0`, which
marching cubes treats as "inside", so the surface normals point outward (the
same signed convention MolecularSurface uses).

## Why the field is local (no box-blob)

The gaussian envelope `exp(-r^2/scale^2)` decays to about `0` well before the
sampling box edge (the box is `center ± 2.5 * scale`, where the envelope is
`exp(-6.25) ~= 0.002`). So `S ~= 0` at the box faces and `f ~= isoValue > 0`
there, which is "outside". The surface closes inside the box and never shuts
against the box faces. MolecularSurface hit that box-blob failure with
a summed metaball field; a decaying envelope avoids it.
examples:
```typescript
const pz = new OrbitalSurface({ type: 'pz', scale: 2 });
scene.add(pz); // a two-color dumbbell along z
```

signatures.summary:
Orient a mesh so its local +Y axis points along a direction.

Three.js cylinders and cones are built along +Y, so a start->end primitive
needs one rotation that maps +Y onto the normalized direction. The rotation
is a quaternion from `setFromUnitVectors`, which itself handles the
antiparallel (-Y) edge case by choosing an orthogonal axis.

A zero-length direction has no orientation, so the mesh is left at identity.

Map a horizontal-space point to the requested orientation.

Horizontal keeps the point. Vertical rotates it so columns run top to bottom,
by the map `(x, y) -> (y, -x)`.

Build an orthographic projection: the view of a globe from infinitely far
away. Only the near hemisphere is mappable; a point on the far hemisphere
(angular distance greater than 90 degrees from the view center) comes back as
`[NaN, NaN]`, so callers drop it (see isProjectedPointVisible).

Spinning-globe pattern: build one projection per frame with a growing
`rotate[0]`, for example `orthographic({ rotate: [frame * 2, 0] })`, and the
globe turns eastward. Two different `rotate` values give two still frames of
that spin.

`x = radius * cos(lat) * sin(lon - centerLon)` and
`y = radius * (cos(centerLat) sin(lat) - sin(centerLat) cos(lat) cos(lon - centerLon))`.

fields.doc:
The geographic point placed at the center of the disc, facing the viewer,

and touch input.

sparks, flow fields and physics demos. Unlike PointCloudDot and other

testable without a GPU. Rendering reuses the PMobject point buffer:

signatures.summary:
Map an evaluated value w = f(z) to an `[r, g, b]` float color (0..1).

The hue encodes arg(w): the positive real axis is hue 0, and a quarter turn
toward the positive imaginary axis shifts the hue by 90 degrees. The modulus
|w| drives brightness through the chosen scheme. The result is always a valid
color: a pole (|w| not finite) reads bright, a zero reads dark, and any
non-finite channel becomes 0, so poles and zeros never produce NaN colors.

symbols.name: PhysicsWorld
symbols.summary:
A compact, self-contained 2D rigid-body physics world.

The world holds Body objects and Constraint objects and
advances them with semi-implicit (symplectic) Euler integration. It mirrors
ParticleSystem: a fixed `seed` drives a `mulberry32` PRNG, so the
simulation is deterministic and reproducible without a GPU, and an updater
added in the constructor steps the world from the scene render loop.

Each body can carry a repo mobject (a Circle, Dot or Polygon). The world
adds that mobject as a child and moves it to the body position on every
step, so adding the world to a scene renders the simulation.

There is no heavy physics dependency. The solver is a few hundred lines of
plain math, split across sibling files (vec2, bodies, constraints,
collisions, builders).

symbols.name: ReactionArrow
symbols.summary:
ReactionArrow - a straight reaction-scheme arrow between chemical species.

A reaction scheme draws a species on the left, an arrow, and a species on the
right: `A + B --cat--> C`. The arrow states the reaction direction and carries
the conditions (catalyst, solvent, heat) above and below its shaft. This is the
straight species-to-species arrow, distinct from the curved
ElectronPushingArrow that shows electron movement inside one mechanism
step.

Four kinds cover the common symbols:
- `'forward'` — one shaft with a single filled head at `end` (A -> B).
- `'reversible'` — two offset parallel shafts, the top head points to `end`,
  the bottom head points to `start`. The standard reversible-reaction symbol.
- `'equilibrium'` — like `'reversible'` but with HALF heads (harpoons). The
  repository has no half-head tip primitive, so each harpoon is drawn as one
  barb stroke (the same single-barb technique the fishhook uses in
  ElectronPushingArrow). The two harpoon barbs sit on opposite sides,
  the conventional equilibrium symbol.
- `'resonance'` — one shaft with a filled head at BOTH ends. The resonance
  symbol between contributing structures.

The object is a VGroup: its children are the shaft Lines, the
head tips, and the optional condition Text labels. So it adds to a
scene and animates with `Create` like any group, and the usual Mobject
transforms position it.

Primitive reuse: shafts are Line, filled heads are
ArrowTriangleFilledTip, condition labels are Text. No arrow
math is reinvented.

symbols.name: ReactionScheme
symbols.summary:
ReactionScheme - a multistep reaction laid out as a horizontal row.

A reaction scheme reads left to right: `A --cond--> B --cond--> C`. This
mobject places each species (MoleculeMobject) in a row and draws a
ReactionArrow in the gap between each adjacent pair. It composes the
two existing chemistry primitives; it reinvents neither the molecule drawing
nor the arrow math.

Layout. The row runs along a single horizontal centerline (y = 0). A cursor
walks left to right. For each species the cursor places the species' bounding
box center at `cursorX + width/2`, so the species' left edge lands on the
cursor. Between two species the cursor leaves `gap`, an arrow of length
`arrowLength`, then another `gap`. So the cursor advances by
`width + gap + arrowLength + gap` per step. The arrow aligns to the same
centerline and carries the step's conditions.

The object is a VGroup: its children are the species and the arrows.
So it adds to a scene and animates with `Create` like any group.

symbols.name: RegularPolygram
symbols.summary:
RegularPolygram - A generalized star polygon {n/k}

Creates a regular star polygon by placing n vertices equally spaced on a
circle and connecting every k-th vertex, where k is the density.

When gcd(n, k) = 1 the result is a single continuous self-intersecting
path that winds k times around the center before closing (e.g. the
pentagram {5/2}).

When gcd(n, k) > 1 the polygram decomposes into gcd(n,k) congruent
regular polygon components, each rendered as a separate child VMobject.
For example, a hexagram {6/2} becomes 2 equilateral triangles (2{3}).

This matches the behavior of Python manim's RegularPolygram.

symbols.summary: Options for creating a RegularPolygram

fields.doc: Center position. Default: [0, 0, 0]

fields.doc: Stroke color as CSS color string. Default: Manim's blue (#58C4DD)

fields.name: density
fields.doc:
Density (vertex step count), i.e. how many vertices to skip when
drawing each edge. Default: 2

The Schlafli symbol {numVertices/density} describes the polygram.
For example {5/2} is a pentagram, {7/3} is a heptagram.

When gcd(numVertices, density) > 1 the polygram decomposes into
multiple congruent regular polygon components. For instance {6/2}
simplifies to 2{3} -- two overlapping equilateral triangles.

symbols.name: SafeArea
symbols.summary:
SafeArea - responsive layout against a common visible rectangle.

Content creators author one scene and render it at several aspect ratios
(16:9 landscape, 9:16 portrait, 1:1 square). The safe area is the rectangle
visible in EVERY target aspect: the intersection of all the target frames at
a shared reference scale. Anchor a mobject to the safe area and it stays on
screen in every aspect ("reflows") instead of being clipped when the author
switches aspect with Scene.setFrameAspect.

The frame model mirrors the camera's `fill` mode (see Camera2D): all
target frames share one reference height, so the frame width tracks the
aspect and the width is the limiting dimension. This keeps the safe area
exact against what the camera actually renders.

signatures.summary:
Select a subset of a parsed structure.

Builds a candidate list of `atoms` plus (when `includeHetatms`, the default)
`hetatms`. It keeps a candidate when every provided filter accepts it, then
inverts the result when `invert` is set. The returned structure is fresh and
the input is not mutated.

Bonds: kept only when both endpoints survive, with `from` / `to` re-numbered
into the new combined space (kept atoms first, then kept hetatms).

Residues: a residue is kept when a kept atom shares its chain and resSeq. For
a residue with no resSeq, it is kept when its CA position coincides with a
kept atom's position.

Degenerate input: an empty selection returns an empty but valid structure and
does not throw. A proximity filter (`nearPoint` / `nearLigand`) with a radius
<= 0 selects nothing.

symbols.summary:

It mirrors the Shadertoy convention with built-in uniforms updated each
frame: `iTime` (seconds), `iResolution` (vec3 plane size), and an optional
`iMouse` (vec4). User uniforms (floats, vectors, colors, textures) pass
through an options map. A frame updater advances `iTime`, so animated
shaders run on the timeline.

Construction never touches a WebGL context, so it is headless-safe; the
material is built lazily on the first getThreeObject call. Uniform
and time updates made before that point are stored and applied on build.

Unlike the DOM `Controls.addSlider` widget, this slider is drawn from
mobjects (a track Line and a draggable handle Dot), so it

symbols.name: SpatialAudio
symbols.summary:
SpatialAudio - Positional (3D) audio for manim-web.

Wraps a Web Audio `PannerNode` so a sound can live at a point in the scene
and pan as it, or the camera, moves. The sound can follow a mobject: on
every `update(dt)` the panner moves to the mobject center, so the standard
updater loop keeps audio and geometry in sync. An `AudioListener` setter
places the listener from the camera, so the mix tracks the point of view.

This is impossible in file-based ManimCE and is browser-unique. It mirrors
AudioAnalyzer: the same feature detection, the same dependency
injection seam, and the same degrade-to-no-op contract.

Every Web Audio and DOM access is feature-detected. In Node, jsdom, or SSR
the class degrades to a no-op: it tracks its position but builds no audio
graph and nothing throws.

signatures.signature: springLayoutStep(vertices: VertexId[], edges: EdgeTuple[], positions: Map<VertexId, SpringPoint>, params: SpringStepParams): SpringStepResult
signatures.summary:
Advance the spring (force-directed) simulation by one step.

This is one Fruchterman-Reingold iteration. It computes repulsive forces
between every pair of vertices and attractive forces along the edges. Then it
moves each vertex by its net force, limited by the temperature. It returns a
new positions map and the cooled temperature, so the caller holds the state.

The function is pure. It reads `positions` and returns new positions. It does
not change the input. Run it `iterations` times to reproduce
`computeSpringLayout`.

fields.doc:
Bounce in [0, 1). 0 gives no overshoot. Values near 1 give large
overshoot. If set, this replaces stiffness and damping.

fields.name: damping
fields.doc: Damping (friction) coefficient. Higher settles faster. Default 10.

fields.name: mass
fields.doc: Mass on the spring. Higher is slower. Default 1.

fields.name: restThreshold
fields.doc:
Settle threshold used to map physical time into [0, 1].
The spring reaches this distance from 1 at t = 1. Default 0.005.

fields.name: stiffness
fields.doc: Spring constant. Higher is tighter. Default 100.

symbols.name: StateMachine
symbols.summary:
StateMachine — a Rive-style, input-driven animation controller.

A machine holds named **states**, typed **inputs** (boolInput,
numberInput, triggerInput) and **transitions** between states
guarded by input conditions. Call update each frame to evaluate the
transitions of the current state. On entering a state the machine runs that
state's `onEnter` action, which is where an animation or a property change
starts. This makes interactive, state-driven animations (hover to expand,
toggle, multi-state UI flows) first-class, which manim-web lacked.

The core logic is headless and deterministic: it reads no DOM and, for the
same input sequence, produces the same state sequence. To drive it from UI
events, pass inputHandler / triggerHandler to a `Clickable`
`onClick`, a `Hoverable` `onHoverStart` / `onHoverEnd`, or a `Slider`
`onChange`.

symbols.name: Text3D
symbols.summary:
Text3D - extruded / beveled 3D text as a mobject.

ManimCE renders only flat Text / MathTex. manim-web adds true 3D text with
depth and an optional bevel through Three.js TextGeometry, which extrudes a
typeface.json font into a solid mesh. The mesh drops into the normal
Mobject3D hierarchy, so it participates in shift / scale / rotate, z-depth and
the 3D camera exactly like a Cube or a Sphere.

Async + dependency-injection design (why there are static factories):
  TextGeometry needs a parsed font, and the font loads over the network with
  the FontLoader example module. Both the import and the load are async, so
  the real path does them in `fromUrl` / `fromFont`, then constructs a Text3D
  with the resolved font and a synchronous geometry factory. The mesh itself
  builds lazily and synchronously in `_createThreeObject`, like ModelMobject.

The example modules are pulled in through a lazy dynamic `import()` on first
use, so the base bundle and SSR never load them. Tests inject a stub font
loader and a recording geometry factory (via the options or the module seams
`setFontLoaderFactory` / `setTextGeometryFactory`), which bypasses the import,
the network and any GPU - mirroring the `setModelLoaderFactory` seam in
ModelMobject.

No large font is bundled. `fromUrl` defaults to DEFAULT_FONT_URL, a
CDN-hosted typeface.json; supply your own `fontUrl` or a parsed `font`.

symbols.name: TextOnPath
symbols.summary:
TextOnPath - lay out glyphs along an arbitrary curve.

A VGroup that places each glyph of a run along a path (an Arc, a Line, a
parametric curve, or any VMobject) by arc length. Each glyph center sits at a
successive arc-length offset (advance width + tracking) and, by default,
rotates to match the path tangent. This is the per-glyph typography layout
that ManimCE's `MoveAlongPath` does not provide (that animates a whole
mobject along a path).

Two construction modes:
  - Synchronous: pass pre-built glyph mobjects with their advance widths.
  - Asynchronous: pass a string plus a font URL; call `waitForReady()`.

The layout math lives in `textOnPathLayout.ts` and is font-free and testable.

symbols.name: TransformMatchingCode
symbols.summary:
TransformMatchingCode - animate between two Code blocks by matching tokens.

ManimCE issue #4103: transforming a Code mobject redraws the whole block
instead of animating only the lines or tokens that changed. This animation
fixes that in the browser, in the spirit of Motion Canvas:

- Unchanged tokens (matched by content) move to their new position.
- Removed tokens (in the source only) fade out.
- Added tokens (in the target only) fade in.

It mirrors the design of TransformMatchingTex and TransformMatchingShapes
(key-based matching, a `keyFunc` override, a `fadeRatio`, and a
`transformMismatches` option) but works at the token/line level of the Code
mobject instead of at the vector-path level, because a Code block renders to
a single texture rather than to per-token submobjects.

symbols.summary:
TransformMatchingShapes animation - transforms matching shapes between mobjects.

Uses the Hungarian algorithm for optimal shape matching:
- When a keyFunc is provided: exact key-based matching (same as before)
- When no keyFunc: builds a similarity matrix and uses the Hungarian algorithm
  to find the globally optimal one-to-one assignment that maximizes total
  similarity, subject to a minimum threshold.

symbols.name: Typst
symbols.summary:
Typst - Vector-based Typst rendering using SVG paths.

`Typst` compiles Typst markup to SVG via a lazy-loaded WASM compiler and
imports the result into real VMobject paths, exactly like `MathTex` does for
LaTeX. This enables path-based animations (Create, DrawBorderThenFill,
point-morphing Transform). `MathTypst` is the math-mode variant: it wraps the
input in Typst math delimiters (`$ ... $`), mirroring the MathTex-vs-Tex split.

Difference from MathTex: the MathJax render path can resolve synchronously in
some environments, while the Typst compiler is ALWAYS asynchronous (the WASM
compile is a promise). Construction stays synchronous; call `waitForRender()`
(the same ready-promise pattern MathTex exposes) before reading geometry.

Uses renderTypstToSVG() -> svgToVMobjects() pipeline.

signatures.summary:
Return a unit vector perpendicular to `n`.

Picked by Gram–Schmidt against whichever world basis vector has the
smallest |dot(n, e_i)|, then normalized. This is coordinate-free in
spirit — it never uses a hard "is the input close to Z?" branch — but it
does pick from the world basis, so the result can change discontinuously
very near a tie. Treat as "give me *some* perpendicular unit vector"
rather than a temporally-stable frame.

Vectorized Mobject - a mobject defined by cubic Bezier curves.
This is the base class for all path-based shapes.

Points are stored as cubic Bezier control points:
[anchor1, handle1, handle2, anchor2, handle3, handle4, anchor3, ...]

Each curve segment uses 4 points: anchor -> handle -> handle -> anchor
Consecutive segments share the anchor point.

symbols.name: WaterfallChart
symbols.summary:
WaterfallChart - A waterfall (bridge) chart mobject.

Shows sequential positive and negative contributions as floating bars. Bar i
starts at the running total of the previous bars and spans its own delta.
Positive and negative deltas use separate colors. Connector lines join each
bar to the next at the running-total level. An optional total bar spans from
zero to the final sum.

The chart is a VGroup, so Create and FadeIn animate it directly.

symbols.name: WaveLetters
symbols.summary:
WaveLetters - an emphasis effect. Each glyph oscillates along a direction
with a per-glyph phase offset, so the group ripples like a wave. An
envelope brings every glyph back to its base position at both ends, so
interpolate(0) and interpolate(1) leave the glyphs unmoved.

fields.name: alpha
fields.doc:
Export with a transparent background, so the video carries an alpha
channel to composite over other footage. Defaults to false.

Alpha needs the 'webm' format with the 'vp9' codec, because only that path
carries an alpha side channel. When `alpha` is set and `format`/`codec` are
not given, they default to 'webm' and 'vp9'. It also needs a Scene created
with `{ alpha: true }` (or `backgroundOpacity < 1`) and a browser that can
encode VP9 with alpha. When any requirement is unmet, `export()` throws a
clear error instead of producing opaque video that claims transparency.

symbols.name: WiggleOutThenIn
symbols.summary:
WiggleOutThenIn animation - wiggles a mobject outward (scaling up with
rotation oscillation) and then back to its original state.

This mimics Manim's WiggleOutThenIn animation. The mobject scales up
to a peak scale factor using a there-and-back envelope, while
simultaneously rotating back and forth with a sine-based oscillation
that starts and ends at zero.

Parameters:
- scaleValue: peak scale factor (default 1.1)
- rotationAngle: maximum rotation in radians (default 0.01 * TAU)
- nWiggles: number of rotation oscillations (default 6)
- rotationAxis: axis to rotate about (default Z axis)

symbols.name: Write
symbols.summary:
Write animation specifically for Text and MathTex mobjects.
Reveals text character by character with a pen-stroke effect.

Rendering paths:
1. Glyph stroke mode — Text with loaded glyph group (via loadGlyphs()) gets stroke-draw
   of each character's outline, then cross-fades to the Canvas 2D texture.
2. Dash-based reveal — for VMobjects that already have Line2 children.
3. Opacity fallback.

fields.doc: Duration of the animation in seconds (default: 1)

fields.name: lagRatio
fields.doc: Stagger between characters, default 0.05

fields.name: rateFunc
fields.doc: Rate function controlling the animation's pacing (default: smooth)

fields.name: remover
fields.doc: Remove after animation, default false

fields.name: reverse
fields.doc: Write in reverse (right to left), default false

fields.name: shift
fields.doc: Shift direction for fade animations

fields.name: strokeRatio
fields.doc: Ratio of animation time spent on stroke drawing vs cross-fade (default 0.7 = 70% stroke, 30% crossfade)

fields.name: useSkeletonStroke
fields.doc:
When true, the Write animation uses the glyph's skeleton (medial axis)
for stroke drawing, producing natural center-line pen strokes instead
of perimeter outlines. Requires glyphs to be loaded with
`useSkeletonStroke: true`. Default: false (uses outline strokes).

symbols.name: ZoomDisplayPopOut
symbols.summary:
Animation that pops the zoomed display out from the camera frame to its
target position, mimicking Manim's get_zoomed_display_pop_out_animation().

In begin(), the display's current position/scale are saved, then the display
is snapped onto the camera frame via replace(frame, stretch=true).
interpolate(alpha) lerps from frame-matched state (alpha=0) to the saved
original state (alpha=1). Works with reversed rate functions for reverse
pop-out.
